summary: Describes the Low Latency, Low Loss, and Scalable throughput (L4S) architecture. It rests on the idea that queuing delay is caused by capacity-seeking congestion controllers at senders, not by the queue itself, and it lets applications transition to scalable congestion control for very low delay. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Waiting lines grow because senders push until the line gets long. L4S has senders ease off a little early and often, so lines stay short.

questions: what is a dual-queue coupled aqm
what is a scalable congestion control
subtitle: Why queues get long, and a plan for senders and routers to keep them short without breaking today's traffic.

tldr.problem: Queuing delay on bottleneck links can reach hundreds of milliseconds, and the RFC argues its root cause is the large sawtooth behavior of Classic congestion controls at senders, which network-side queue management alone cannot fix.
tldr.mechanism: L4S combines Scalable congestion controls in hosts, a separate queue (such as a Dual-Queue Coupled AQM) that isolates low-latency traffic, and the ECT(1) ECN codepoint to tell the network which packets are L4S.
tldr.outcome: The aim is queuing delay under 1 ms on average and about 2 ms at the 99th percentile, with low congestion loss, while typically not hurting Classic traffic. The RFC is informational and the protocol itself is defined separately in RFC 9331.

today: RFC 9330 is an Informational RFC from January 2023, and its metadata shows no obsoleting or updating RFCs. It describes the architecture, while the identifier protocol is defined as an experimental change to ECN in RFC 9331 and the Dual-Queue AQM in RFC 9332.

sections.title: The Queuing Delay Problem
sections.content:
More and more traffic at a bottleneck link, such as a household's access link or Wi-Fi, comes from delay-sensitive applications: interactive web, voice, video calls, cloud gaming, remote desktop and similar. Propagation delay has been reduced by moving caches and servers closer to users, but queuing delay remains a major, intermittent part of latency, with spikes of hundreds of milliseconds even under state-of-the-art Active Queue Management (AQM).

The goal of this RFC is an Internet service with very low queuing latency (less than 1 ms on average and less than about 2 ms at the 99th percentile), very low loss and scalable throughput. Its key claim is that the root of the problem is the Classic congestion controls (Reno and compatible ones such as CUBIC) in senders, which cause large sawtooth swings in queue occupancy. A network operator who simply sets an AQM to a shallower queue would make Classic flows underuse the link.
sections.eli5: Long waiting lines are mostly caused by how people in the line behave, not by the doorway. Fixing the doorway alone does not help enough.

sections.title: The Three Components
sections.content:
The main point is that low latency is not provided by the network. It results from the careful behavior of Scalable congestion controllers at L4S senders. The network's role is to isolate that low latency from the larger queue that Classic traffic needs, and to signal the very start of queue growth immediately using ECN.

The architecture has three parts: host (a Scalable congestion control such as DCTCP or its descendant Prague), network (an AQM that keeps L4S and Classic traffic in separate treatments) and protocol (an identifier in the IP header so the network can tell the two apart). The RFC defines a Scalable congestion control as one where the average time between congestion signals stays the same as the flow rate grows. DCTCP, for instance, averages 2 congestion signals per round trip at any rate.
sections.eli5: Three helpers work together: the sender who eases off early, the road with a fast lane, and a sticker on each message saying which lane it wants.

sections.title: Network and Host Mechanisms
sections.content:
L4S uses the ECN field in the IP header. The ECT(1) codepoint identifies L4S packets, and the CE codepoint signals congestion for both treatments. ECT(1) had been assigned to the experimental ECN nonce; RFC 8311 recategorizes that as historic and relaxes the Classic ECN rule that a mark must be treated like a drop, so L4S marks can be more frequent and immediate.

In the network, the main design is the Dual-Queue Coupled AQM (specified in RFC 9332). It uses two queues for latency isolation, while the Classic queue's AQM also feeds a coupled signal to the L4S queue so that both kinds of flow get roughly equal throughput without identifying individual flows. The scheduler serves the L4S queue with priority, which the RFC advises should be conditional, not strict. Other arrangements are per-flow queues (such as FQ-CoDel with a shallow threshold applied to ECT(1) packets) and dual queues with per-flow AQMs.

In the host, senders need a Scalable congestion control and feedback fine-grained enough to carry it. DCCP and QUIC already provide that, TCP needs more accurate ECN feedback (AccECN), and SCTP would need a new design. For RTP, the RFC points to the feedback defined in RFC 6679 and the newer RFC 8888.
sections.eli5: The network keeps two lines: a short fast one for careful senders and a longer one for everyone else. A link between the lines keeps them fair to each other.

sections.title: Why These Choices
sections.content:
The RFC argues that explicit congestion signals can be used many times per round trip and be sent immediately, which a drop cannot because a drop is also an impairment. It also shifts smoothing from the network, which would have to assume a worst-case round-trip time and so delays Classic signals by 100-200 ms, to each host, which knows its own RTT and usually needs only a few milliseconds.

It illustrates the scaling problem with Reno at a maximum RTT of 30 ms. When the packet rate grows 8 times from 1,250 to 10,000 packets per second, the recovery time after a congestion event also grows 8 times, from 422 ms to 3.38 s. A Scalable control keeps its 2 signals per round trip whatever the rate.

L4S is presented as complementary to existing tools rather than a replacement. It addresses only queuing latency, not bandwidth priority like Diffserv. It adds to state-of-the-art AQMs, to per-flow queuing and to Alternative Back-off ECN, and BBRv2 can use L4S ECN. The Dual-Queue form needs no inspection above the IP layer, so it works with end-to-end encryption.
sections.eli5: A shout of "slow down a bit" works better early and often than a loud stop after things have gone wrong. L4S lets the network shout early.

sections.title: Incremental Deployment
sections.content:
L4S is designed to be deployed step by step. Access networks usually have one known bottleneck link per site, so deploying an L4S AQM at each end of that link should give nearly all of the benefit in each direction. Mesh networks depend on how overbooked the core is.

For one flow to benefit, three parts may be needed: a Scalable sender, an L4S AQM at the bottleneck, and, for TCP, upgraded receiver feedback. The RFC suggests a sequence that starts with controlled trials using DCTCP, which already exists on many hosts, then moves to TCP Prague and AccECN feedback, then to the upstream direction. QUIC's feedback has supported L4S from the outset.

If an L4S flow meets a bottleneck with no ECN support, the sender must respond to loss as safely as Classic traffic does, which degrades the L4S service to no better than Classic best effort. The RFC lists approaches to improve this as research in progress. It also notes that an AQM inside a tunnel needs standards-compliant propagation of the ECN field.
sections.eli5: Nobody has to rebuild the whole road at once. Fix the one narrow spot near each home and most of the benefit shows up straight away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security discussion centers on whether L4S traffic needs policing. The RFC says the internet has always relied on the self-restraint of congestion controls at senders, that L4S is designed not to upset this, and that the Dual-Queue design gives no more rate advantage to unresponsive flows than a single-queue AQM would. Networks that do not offer L4S are required not to change the L4S identifier and can treat the traffic like Not-ECT.

Because L4S also needs senders to limit burstiness, a malicious or buggy flow could attack the low latency of the shared queue. The RFC lists possible protections, including per-flow queue protection (developed for DOCSIS), reactive traffic scrubbing, per-flow scheduling and edge conditioning. Operators may also restrict L4S to selected customers by combining a local classifier with the ECN identifier. The document also covers ECN integrity and privacy considerations.
sections.eli5: Because the fast lane is only for careful senders, someone could try to cheat by rushing in. The paper lists guards a network can add if cheating becomes a problem.

items.title: Host
items.text: A Scalable congestion control such as DCTCP or Prague reacts to frequent ECN signals and keeps queues short.

items.title: Network
items.text: An AQM isolates L4S traffic from Classic traffic, for example with a Dual-Queue Coupled AQM.

items.title: Protocol
items.text: The ECT(1) codepoint in the IP ECN field identifies L4S packets; CE signals congestion.
